39	# Reconstructing the item
40	
41	**Slice boundary.** Recover what a work item is for — its goal, its problem, and the
42	obligations that would settle it — and produce one `interpretation` artifact corroborated by a
43	second independent reading, or stop with the drafted interpretation as the run's product.
44	
45	| | |
46	| --- | --- |
47	| Ships | `lib/lint-interpretation.js` · the Author's blind-read prompt · the Boundary-reviewer's blind-read prompt · this document |
48	| Gating test | *planned* — `npx jest modus/lib/__tests__/lint-interpretation.test.js`. Exact finding-set assertions over the interpretation fixtures, the five assertion-versus-absence portability assertions, and a prompt template contract asserting every placeholder binds and the declared output shape validates against the linter's input schema |
49	| Non-gating | Model eval over `tests/transcriptions/` · offline hand-grading of the reconstruction against what the requester actually wanted |
50	| Depends on | [`tracker-and-forge-ports`](tracker-and-forge-ports.md) — `read(ref)` must return addressable parts, or every `item_locator` has nothing to resolve against |
51	| Terminal failure owned | `X_GAP_UNRESOLVABLE`, `X_QUANTITY_ASSUMED`, `X_CORRECTION_CHANGES_SCOPE`, `X_RECONSTRUCTION_UNANCHORED`, `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED`, `X_MOVES_SURFACE_DISPUTED` — all reaching the `interpretation_blocked` stop state |
52	| Source lines | 90-199, 234-237, 275-292, 350-430, 447-461, 606-614, 639-647, 660-681 of the pre-split `autonomous-workitem-workflow.md` |
53	
54	GOAL: Recover the item's goal, the problem it is solving, and the obligations that would settle
55	it, with every part declaring whether the item stated it, the repository supplied it, or the two
56	disagree.
57	HOW: Read the item alone first and record what it says, each part carrying a locator. Then
58	resolve those claims against the repository, logs, and history, and set provenance from that
59	resolution. A second reader reconstructs the item blind, and the two readings are compared before
60	either is trusted.
61	JUSTIFICATION: The item is unrefined, so obligations have to be reconstructed rather than
62	transcribed. -- (RubricBench `:151` -- models "fail to define the necessary constraints on their
63	own", 27% gap against human rubrics; `:1172` -- a model-authored rubric on an ill-posed task
64	"devolves into a standard implementation checklist" and penalises correct refusal)
65	IMPACT: high -- this is the ceiling on every slice after it.
66	
67	This slice owns the `interpretation` contract. [`the-boundary-bundle`](the-boundary-bundle.md)
68	consumes it by reference and does not restate its schema.
69	
70	## The item is evidence, not a specification
71	
72	Real trackers hold unrefined, incorrect, and incomplete items. Acceptance criteria fit to serve as an
73	autonomous completion metric are the exception, not the input. So the first real job of a run is to
74	recover the item's **goal**, the **problem** it is solving, and the **obligations** that would settle
75	it — and that reconstruction, not the implementation, is where most runs will fail.
76	
77	This is measured rather than assumed. Given an ill-posed task — "convert SQL to Mongo for all cases" —
78	a model-authored rubric "devolves into a standard implementation checklist", then penalises a correct
79	refusal for "missing code" while rewarding a hallucinated solution
80	(`rubric-limits--zhang-2026--rubricbench:1172`). The failure is not that the model reconstructed the
81	criteria badly. It is that the model reconstructed *implementable* criteria from an item that had
82	none, and everything downstream then verified against them faithfully.
83	
84	Four failure modes, and they need different handling, because conflating them yields either a
85	workflow that never starts or one that confidently ships the wrong feature. This table is the only
86	place they are enumerated; the schema section below names the fields and does not restate the modes.
87	
88	| Mode | Item against repository | Handling | Code | Reason code |
89	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
90	| **Underspecified** | omits something the repository, logs, or history can settle | fill it, record what it was filled from, proceed — the common case, and treating it as an error means nothing ever runs | — | — |
91	| **Unsettleable** | omits something nothing available can settle | terminal; filling it injects an assumption | `X_GAP_UNRESOLVABLE`, `X_QUANTITY_ASSUMED` | `underdetermined_by_issue` |
92	| **Contradicted** | asserts something the repository shows is false | proceed when the correction does not move the change surface; terminal when it does | `X_CORRECTION_CHANGES_SCOPE` | `item_correction_changes_scope` |
93	| **Unanchored** | nothing states what the item is for, and the repository cannot supply it | halts the spend and routes to the independent reconstruction; terminal only once that corroborates it | `X_RECONSTRUCTION_UNANCHORED` → `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED` | `item_unanchored` |
94	
95	Underspecified and unsettleable were one row in an earlier draft, which hid the fact that the
96	interesting boundary is not whether the item is silent but whether anything else can speak.
97	
98	The last row is two codes because it is two claims. "Nothing in *this reconstruction* is anchored"
99	is what one artifact can support; "nothing in *the item* is anchored" needs a second, independent
100	reading to agree. An earlier draft collapsed them and ended the run at stage 2 — with the artifact
101	that distinguishes them specified, evaluated, and ordered out of reach.
102	
103	Filling a gap is not free, and the corpus names the way it goes wrong. On an underspecified instruction
104	missing a required interest rate, the human rubric required the model to ask; the model-authored rubric
105	instead "validates the correctness of the math performed on arbitrary assumptions (e.g., 3%)",
106	penalising the honest response and rewarding the invented one — the paper's **False Precision Bias**
107	(`rubric-limits:1278`). An obligation carrying a number the item never supplied and the repository
108	cannot produce is that failure exactly.
109	
110	The mechanical counterpart is `quantity.filled_from`, required on every quantitative entry, and it
111	lives on the quantity rather than in a list somewhere else in the manifest. An earlier draft claimed
112	the `gaps[]` entry did this work — the worked example's `AC-1` asserts 240 seconds against an item with
113	no number in it, and the document said that without the gaps entry the threshold "is an assumption
114	wearing a `quantity` object". That was false: emptying `gaps[]` left `AC-1` standing and the manifest
115	clean, because nothing connected a quantity to the gap that filled it. Provenance has to be recorded at
116	the point of use or it is a parallel record that enforces nothing.
117	
118	Escalating an unanchored item is not an admission of defeat. PaperBench hit the same wall and answered
119	it the same way: "To deal with underspecification, we collaborate with authors from the papers to make
120	specific choices about what is important", noting that "there exist many different realizations of our
121	paper rubrics which are no less valid"
122	(`rubric-impl--starace-2025-openai--paperbench:1447`). Where several readings are equally valid,
123	choosing one is a decision with an owner, and the owner is not this run. The run's product in that case
124	is the drafted interpretation, attached to the item through `attach_reference`.
125	
126	**The escalation cannot be the reconstructing model's judgment call, and this design does not fully
127	achieve that.** RubricBench's execution-failure analysis finds that models "struggle to operationalize
128	rubric-implied behaviors such as abstention or rejection when tasks are indeterminate or infeasible"
129	even when handed correct human rubrics (`rubric-limits:1289`) — abstention is the specific thing they
130	are measured to be bad at. What the interpretation block buys is narrower than mechanical adjudication:
131	the model's judgment becomes a **declared field with a mechanical consequence**. No script can decide
132	whether a correction moves the change surface, but once the Author declares that it does, the run is
133	over — terminal, non-retryable, no lint-round loop, no second opinion from the actor that benefits from
134	a different answer. The declaration is self-serving to under-report, and its only counterweight is the
135	independent reconstruction below — which is a counterweight only because the two sides' `moves_surface`
136	declarations are actually **compared**. For one round they were not: the field was read in a single place,
137	the pair pass never looked at `corrections[]`, and the common case — a blind reviewer that never
138	rediscovers the contradiction — was clean. A declared field with a mechanical consequence and no
139	cross-check is the unfalsifiable claim moved one field over, which is the same defect as deciding
140	provenance by how an id is spelled.
141	
142	**Terminal findings are protected by two policies, both the same principle.** First, a terminal
143	conclusion may not be drawn from a document that has retryable defects: four capitalisation typos on
144	provenance values used to produce a terminal stop, because the enum check returned before the anchor was
145	counted. The guard is uniform over a pass rather than attached to each check, because the previous
146	version *was* attached to one check and missed the next case. Second, terminals are evaluated on the
147	Author's interpretation; a reviewer that anchors nothing produces
148	`E_REVIEWER_RECONSTRUCTION_UNUSABLE` and a fresh-reviewer retry, not a stop that blames the item.
149	
150	That second policy needs a distinction to be correct rather than merely safe, and the first version of
151	it was wrong. Suppressing the reviewer's terminals wholesale discards the reviewer's `moves_surface: true`,
152	which is precisely the input the cross-side check consumes — the two fixes cancelled. The criterion that
153	makes both work is **assertion versus absence**, and it is decidable from the source rather than from a
154	judgment about what a code is "about":
155	
156	| Trigger | Fires on | Portable between artifacts |
157	| --- | --- | --- |
158	| `assertion` | a value the Author wrote — `moves_surface: true`, `filled_from: unresolved`, two written values differing | yes; an assertion is attributable, so it means the same thing wherever it is found |
159	| `absence` | nothing written — no part declared `stated` or `stated_unverified` | no; "the item states nothing" and "this reading found nothing" are indistinguishable from one artifact |
160	
161	An earlier version of this split keyed on "the reconstruction's own adequacy versus a property of the
162	item". That classified the same codes correctly and was undecidable from the source — and the tell was
163	that it called `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED` an adequacy code while the code's own name, its message, and the
164	failure-mode table all called it a property of the item. Three places said item, the list said adequacy.
165	That was a naming bug rather than a classification bug: the two readings are now two codes, and each
166	name is accurate.
167	
168	Every terminal code declares its trigger, and the suite tests the declaration against behaviour with
169	five portability assertions — because an assertion in a comment is the same shape as the exemption that
170	hid a bug for two commits.
171	
172	**This is not a separate stage.** It is what stage 2 was already doing, named, plus one comparison at
173	the review-and-freeze step. Reconstruction has a decent claim to its own persisted state, but the
174	promotion rule wants a diagnosed failure class across two pilot runs and there have been no pilot runs.
175	
176	The honest counterweight belongs next to that, as the thing to watch: reconstruction now has its own
177	linter pass, its own actor pair, its own code prefix, its own escalation family, and its own stop state,
178	and it is the largest thing inside any stage. If a pilot diagnoses a reconstruction failure class twice,
179	the promotion evidence will already be sitting here.
180	
181	### The reconstruction is the ceiling on everything after it
182	
183	Every slice after this one verifies against the frozen bundle, so a faithful implementation of a wrong
184	reconstruction passes every gate and reports `ready_for_merge`. TICK gives that outcome its shape: a
185	response that fabricated its sources answered 9 of 10 generated checklist questions YES and scored 2/5
186	from a human annotator (`checklist--cook-2024:1961`), because the generated checklist inherited the
187	instruction's false premise (`:1878`).
188	
189	The authors' conclusion has to be quoted whole, because an earlier version of this section cut it in a
190	direction that flattered the argument. It reads: generated-checklist answers "alone should not be used
191	to score responses **in human evaluation**, but also showing that **human evaluators are robust to
192	unhelpful or misleading checklists**" (`:1883`). Both restored clauses matter. The scope qualifier is
193	material — the finding is about human annotators working from a generated checklist, whereas this
194	pipeline's gates are mechanical checks and a model reviewer, so "this workflow does exactly that" was
195	too quick. And the second clause is evidence *for* one of the three mitigations rather than against it:
196	the annotator scored 2/5 correctly while answering 9 of 10 YES, which is the offline hand-graded sample
197	working. Independent reconstruction, declared support, and that sample are the mitigations; none is a
198	solution, and the sample is the one with a data point behind it.
199	
200	## The `interpretation` block
201	
202	It is carried inside the manifest rather than in a side file because it is normative. `claims[]`
203	descend from it, and freezing a bundle whose reconstruction was not frozen with it would leave the
204	run's definition of the goal mutable after the freeze. The manifest that carries it is defined in
205	[`the-boundary-bundle`](the-boundary-bundle.md); the block's own schema is defined here and is not
206	restated there.
207	
208	| Field | Contents |
209	| --- | --- |
210	| `goal.statement`, `problem.statement` | What the item is for; what is wrong or missing now |
211	| `provenance` on each | `stated` \| `stated_unverified` \| `inferred` \| `contradicted` |
212	| `support[]` on each | Typed pointers, below |
213	| `claim_provenance{}` | Keyed by claim id, valued by the same `provenance` plus `support[]` shape |
214	| `corrections[]` | One per place the item asserts something the repository contradicts |
215	| `gaps[]` | One per element the item did not supply |
216	
217	`claim_provenance` is a map rather than a field on each claim for a reason that is not cosmetic: the
218	same block is written by two actors. The Author writes one into the manifest, and the
219	Boundary-reviewer writes a **standalone** one at the review step with no entries and no claims list. One
220	shape means one set of rules and one linter for both, and it means the reviewer's artifact is not a
221	partial boundary.
222	
223	The provenance values:
224	
225	| Value | Means | Requires |
226	| --- | --- | --- |
227	| `stated` | the item says it and resolution corroborated it | at least one `item_locator` |
228	| `stated_unverified` | the item says it and resolution could neither corroborate nor contradict it | at least one `item_locator`, and no external support — the absence is the point |
229	| `inferred` | the repository, logs, or history supply it | at least one pointer that is **not** an `item_locator` |
230	| `contradicted` | the item asserts it and the repository shows otherwise | as `inferred`, plus a matching `corrections[]` entry |
231	
232	Support pointers are typed, because an untyped citation is unverifiable: `item_locator`, `repo_path`,
233	`log_query`, `commit`, `registry_entry`. The two rules that follow are the ones that do the work — a
234	`stated` claim must carry an `item_locator`, and an inference whose only support is the item it was not
235	in cites nothing.
236	
237	**A locator is checked for presence, never for resolution, and that is the weakest point in the whole
238	provenance system.** The Linter does not read the item — it cannot, since the item lives behind a
239	tracker adapter — so `description#4` on a two-paragraph item lints exactly as clean as a true citation.
240	Every rule here establishes that a citation was *written*, not that it points at anything. The domain
241	that would make resolution checkable is supplied by the tracker adapter and is specified in
242	[`tracker-and-forge-ports`](tracker-and-forge-ports.md).
243	
244	The consequence is worse than "cheap to fake by accident", which is how an earlier version of this
245	paragraph put it. The check did not merely fail to detect divergence — it **affirmatively reported
246	concurrence**. An author reading of "exports are too slow for large accounts" and a reviewer reading of
247	"the retry button double-submits and corrupts the manifest", both citing `description#1`, recorded a
248	`pass`, and the stage reads that as *the two readings are anchored together*. The
249	manufactured-agreement failure, reproduced inside the check built to detect it.
250	
251	Two fixes, and neither needs the adapter. **This check now refutes or abstains and never passes** — a
252	`pass` was the only affirmatively misleading outcome available to it. And the existing exemption is
253	widened rather than joined by a new rule: it already abstains when either side cites nothing, on the
254	grounds that the comparison has no domain, and one identical locator on each side is the same
255	condition — a set with no discriminating power, where identical and opposite readings are
256	indistinguishable.
257	
258	Resolving locators against a real part list, once the adapter supplies one, does **not** rescue the
259	degenerate overlap case. Two reconstructions both citing a *valid* `description#1` are still
260	indistinguishable from each other, which is why `abstain` exists and why there is still no diversity
261	metric.
262	
263	Two residuals, stated rather than checked. A side resting on one locator while the other cites three
264	still reports overlap; drawing that line needs a diversity metric, and the semantic differential is the
265	real check rather than something worth propping up. And a whole interpretation — goal, problem, and
266	every claim — can rest on one default locator with nothing flagging it.
267	
268	`corrections[]` carries `about` (a claim id or the literal `goal` or `problem`), `item_assertion`,
269	`repo_finding`, `support[]`, `resolution` (`item_wrong` | `repo_changed_since` | `ambiguous`), and
270	`moves_surface`. `gaps[]` carries `element` and `filled_from`, which is either a support pointer or the
271	literal `unresolved`.
272	
273	**`stated_unverified` constrains the obligation graph.** A `must` that traces a `stated_unverified`
274	claim **at all** is rejected: it gates partly on an item assertion nothing corroborates. Verify the
275	claim, drop the trace if a coupling edge is the real anchor, or author the obligation as `watch`.
276	
277	The predicate is "cites an uncorroborated claim" and not "has no corroborated anchor", because the
278	weaker form was defeated by adding a single coupling-edge trace — and since `entails` requires every
279	coupling edge to be covered, coupling traces are the normal case rather than an exotic one. The prose
280	said the rule caught a must that gates on an uncorroborated assertion; the code asked whether the entry
281	had any corroborated anchor at all. Those differ exactly when an entry has both, and a coupling edge is
282	a different anchor rather than corroboration of the claim.
283	
284	That member and that rule came out of transcribing the pre-schema worked example, which carried
285	`regression since ~July — unverified secondhand`. A three-member enum could record the first half of
286	that sentence and not the second, so an assertion resolution could not confirm looked identical to one
287	it did. The source had already solved the consequence without naming the cause: its `C2` grounds a
288	`watch` entry and gates nothing.
289	
290	`filled_from: unresolved` means **established** unsettleable and never "not filled in yet", so it
291	requires a non-empty `sought[]` of typed pointers that were checked and did not settle it. Without that
292	the literal did double duty and an honest first-draft placeholder ended the run with no round available
293	to replace it — while a *wrong* pointer continued it. A missing `sought[]` is retryable, which the
294	suppression policy then keeps from terminating.
295	
296	`W_ANCHOR_DISJOINT` is the one warning. Two reconstructions citing no item locator in common may be
297	reading different requirements, but locator overlap is not reading agreement in either direction, and no
298	authoring round can fix a disjoint reading. So it is recorded and requires the semantic divergence test
299	rather than standing in for it.
300	
301	## In the run
302	
303	The Author's pass, before any mechanism work is paid for:
304	
305	- Author: reads the item alone and records what it says — goal, problem, numbered claims — each with an `item_locator` pointing at the part of the item that says it
306	- Author: does this pass first and separately because provenance is otherwise unrecoverable — read the item and the repository together and nothing afterwards can say which of them told you
307	- Author: resolves each claim against read-only repo, logs, and deploy history; quantifies vague terms from data
308	- Author: sets provenance from that resolution — `stated` where corroborated, `stated_unverified` where neither corroborated nor contradicted, `contradicted` where the repository shows otherwise — and adds `inferred` entries for anything the item never mentioned
309	- Author: writes one `corrections[]` entry per contradicted part, naming the item's assertion, the repository's finding, its support, a resolution, and whether the correction **moves the change surface**
310	- Author: writes one `gaps[]` entry per element the item did not supply, naming what it was filled from, or the literal `unresolved` where nothing can settle it
311	- Linter (no model): lints the interpretation on its own, before any mechanism work is paid for, and reports terminal findings separately from fixable ones
312	- Orchestrator (no model): on an **assertion**-triggered terminal finding — appends the reason code, calls `attach_reference` so the drafted interpretation reaches the item as the run's product, finalizes the lease, stops; it consumes no lint round, because no further authoring round can change it
313	- Orchestrator (no model): on the **provisional** finding that nothing in the reconstruction is anchored — skips the mechanism sketch, the coupling analysis, and the registry pass, and goes straight to the independent reading with the interpretation alone; the spend stops here and the run does not
314	
315	The independent reading, which is the counterweight the whole slice rests on:
316	
317	- Orchestrator (no model): starts Boundary-reviewer in a fresh session, cross-family from the Author
318	- Orchestrator (no model): gives it the item text and read-only repo access and **withholds the boundary**, so its reading of the item is not anchored on the Author's
319	- Boundary-reviewer: writes its own standalone `interpretation` — goal, problem, claims, provenance, typed support — under the same rules and the same linter
320	- Linter (no model): lints the reviewer's side under the same rules; where the Author anchored and the reviewer did not, that is `E_REVIEWER_RECONSTRUCTION_UNUSABLE` and a fresh-reviewer retry, because an absence on the reviewer's side is a statement about the reviewer
321	- Linter (no model): resolves the Author's provisional absence against the reviewer's — **both unanchored** is `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED`, corroborated by two blind cross-family readings and now genuinely a property of the item; **Author unanchored, reviewer anchored** is `E_AUTHOR_RECONSTRUCTION_INADEQUATE`, and the Author re-authors against the reviewer's locators
322	- Linter (no model): does not call the reviewer's absence a reviewer defect when the Author is also unanchored, because there it is the corroboration rather than an indictment — treating it as a defect made it a retryable finding, which then suppressed the very conclusion it corroborates
323	- Linter (no model): compares the two — warns `W_ANCHOR_DISJOINT` when their `stated` and `stated_unverified` parts cite no item locator in common, and reports `X_MOVES_SURFACE_DISPUTED` when the two sides disagree about whether correcting the same thing moves the change surface
324	- Boundary-reviewer: then receives the Author's interpretation and describes one change that satisfies its own reading of the goal while failing the Author's, or returns `readings_agree`
325	- Orchestrator (no model): on a described divergence — escalates `intent_ambiguous` and attaches both interpretations; two defensible readings mean the choice between them has an owner
326	
327	> **The divergence test is weak, the calibration is a guess, and the guess was anchored to the wrong
328	> condition.** Song reports two numbers. Where evaluators generate rubrics independently *including
329	> their structure*, "agreement collapses to near-random levels (r̄ ≈ 0.24)"
330	> (`judge-ceiling--song-2026-tencent--evaluation-illusion:87`); standardising the instrument alone

333	> But this design **mandates a shared instrument**: both sides use the same `interpretation` shape, the

335	> 0.24 one.

338	> so the test could afford to be stronger than it is — the escalate-everything fear was calibrated to a
339	> condition this design does not create. And `readings_agree` is **weaker** evidence than a first reading
340	> suggests: Song's point is that 62% of agreement is attributable to the shared instrument rather than
341	> shared judgment, so agreement between two sides using an identical schema is substantially

# Reconstructing the item

**Slice boundary.** Recover what a work item is for — its goal, its problem, and the
obligations that would settle it — and produce one `interpretation` artifact corroborated by a
second independent reading, or stop with the drafted interpretation as the run's product.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Ships | `lib/lint-interpretation.js` · the Author's blind-read prompt · the Boundary-reviewer's blind-read prompt · this document |
| Gating test | *planned* — `npx jest modus/lib/__tests__/lint-interpretation.test.js`. Exact finding-set assertions over the interpretation fixtures, the five assertion-versus-absence portability assertions, and a prompt template contract asserting every placeholder binds and the declared output shape validates against the linter's input schema |
| Non-gating | Model eval over `tests/transcriptions/` · offline hand-grading of the reconstruction against what the requester actually wanted |
| Depends on | [`tracker-and-forge-ports`](tracker-and-forge-ports.md) — `read(ref)` must return addressable parts, or every `item_locator` has nothing to resolve against |
| Terminal failure owned | `X_GAP_UNRESOLVABLE`, `X_QUANTITY_ASSUMED`, `X_CORRECTION_CHANGES_SCOPE`, `X_RECONSTRUCTION_UNANCHORED`, `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED`, `X_MOVES_SURFACE_DISPUTED` — all reaching the `interpretation_blocked` stop state |
| Source lines | 90-199, 234-237, 275-292, 350-430, 447-461, 606-614, 639-647, 660-681 of the pre-split `autonomous-workitem-workflow.md` |

GOAL: Recover the item's goal, the problem it is solving, and the obligations that would settle
it, with every part declaring whether the item stated it, the repository supplied it, or the two
disagree.
HOW: Read the item alone first and record what it says, each part carrying a locator. Then
resolve those claims against the repository, logs, and history, and set provenance from that
resolution. A second reader reconstructs the item blind, and the two readings are compared before
either is trusted.
JUSTIFICATION: The item is unrefined, so obligations have to be reconstructed rather than
transcribed. -- (RubricBench `:151` -- models "fail to define the necessary constraints on their
own", 27% gap against human rubrics; `:1172` -- a model-authored rubric on an ill-posed task
"devolves into a standard implementation checklist" and penalises correct refusal)
IMPACT: high -- this is the ceiling on every slice after it.

This slice owns the `interpretation` contract. [`the-boundary-bundle`](the-boundary-bundle.md)
consumes it by reference and does not restate its schema.

## The item is evidence, not a specification

Real trackers hold unrefined, incorrect, and incomplete items. Acceptance criteria fit to serve as an
autonomous completion metric are the exception, not the input. So the first real job of a run is to
recover the item's **goal**, the **problem** it is solving, and the **obligations** that would settle
it — and that reconstruction, not the implementation, is where most runs will fail.

This is measured rather than assumed. Given an ill-posed task — "convert SQL to Mongo for all cases" —
a model-authored rubric "devolves into a standard implementation checklist", then penalises a correct
refusal for "missing code" while rewarding a hallucinated solution
(`rubric-limits--zhang-2026--rubricbench:1172`). The failure is not that the model reconstructed the
criteria badly. It is that the model reconstructed *implementable* criteria from an item that had
none, and everything downstream then verified against them faithfully.

Four failure modes, and they need different handling, because conflating them yields either a
workflow that never starts or one that confidently ships the wrong feature. This table is the only
place they are enumerated; the schema section below names the fields and does not restate the modes.

| Mode | Item against repository | Handling | Code | Reason code |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Underspecified** | omits something the repository, logs, or history can settle | fill it, record what it was filled from, proceed — the common case, and treating it as an error means nothing ever runs | — | — |
| **Unsettleable** | omits something nothing available can settle | terminal; filling it injects an assumption | `X_GAP_UNRESOLVABLE`, `X_QUANTITY_ASSUMED` | `underdetermined_by_issue` |
| **Contradicted** | asserts something the repository shows is false | proceed when the correction does not move the change surface; terminal when it does | `X_CORRECTION_CHANGES_SCOPE` | `item_correction_changes_scope` |
| **Unanchored** | nothing states what the item is for, and the repository cannot supply it | halts the spend and routes to the independent reconstruction; terminal only once that corroborates it | `X_RECONSTRUCTION_UNANCHORED` → `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED` | `item_unanchored` |

Underspecified and unsettleable were one row in an earlier draft, which hid the fact that the
interesting boundary is not whether the item is silent but whether anything else can speak.

The last row is two codes because it is two claims. "Nothing in *this reconstruction* is anchored"
is what one artifact can support; "nothing in *the item* is anchored" needs a second, independent
reading to agree. An earlier draft collapsed them and ended the run at stage 2 — with the artifact
that distinguishes them specified, evaluated, and ordered out of reach.

Filling a gap is not free, and the corpus names the way it goes wrong. On an underspecified instruction
missing a required interest rate, the human rubric required the model to ask; the model-authored rubric
instead "validates the correctness of the math performed on arbitrary assumptions (e.g., 3%)",
penalising the honest response and rewarding the invented one — the paper's **False Precision Bias**
(`rubric-limits:1278`). An obligation carrying a number the item never supplied and the repository
cannot produce is that failure exactly.

The mechanical counterpart is `quantity.filled_from`, required on every quantitative entry, and it
lives on the quantity rather than in a list somewhere else in the manifest. An earlier draft claimed
the `gaps[]` entry did this work — the worked example's `AC-1` asserts 240 seconds against an item with
no number in it, and the document said that without the gaps entry the threshold "is an assumption
wearing a `quantity` object". That was false: emptying `gaps[]` left `AC-1` standing and the manifest
clean, because nothing connected a quantity to the gap that filled it. Provenance has to be recorded at
the point of use or it is a parallel record that enforces nothing.

Escalating an unanchored item is not an admission of defeat. PaperBench hit the same wall and answered
it the same way: "To deal with underspecification, we collaborate with authors from the papers to make
specific choices about what is important", noting that "there exist many different realizations of our
paper rubrics which are no less valid"
(`rubric-impl--starace-2025-openai--paperbench:1447`). Where several readings are equally valid,
choosing one is a decision with an owner, and the owner is not this run. The run's product in that case
is the drafted interpretation, attached to the item through `attach_reference`.

**The escalation cannot be the reconstructing model's judgment call, and this design does not fully
achieve that.** RubricBench's execution-failure analysis finds that models "struggle to operationalize
rubric-implied behaviors such as abstention or rejection when tasks are indeterminate or infeasible"
even when handed correct human rubrics (`rubric-limits:1289`) — abstention is the specific thing they
are measured to be bad at. What the interpretation block buys is narrower than mechanical adjudication:
the model's judgment becomes a **declared field with a mechanical consequence**. No script can decide
whether a correction moves the change surface, but once the Author declares that it does, the run is
over — terminal, non-retryable, no lint-round loop, no second opinion from the actor that benefits from
a different answer. The declaration is self-serving to under-report, and its only counterweight is the
independent reconstruction below — which is a counterweight only because the two sides' `moves_surface`
declarations are actually **compared**. For one round they were not: the field was read in a single place,
the pair pass never looked at `corrections[]`, and the common case — a blind reviewer that never
rediscovers the contradiction — was clean. A declared field with a mechanical consequence and no
cross-check is the unfalsifiable claim moved one field over, which is the same defect as deciding
provenance by how an id is spelled.

**Terminal findings are protected by two policies, both the same principle.** First, a terminal
conclusion may not be drawn from a document that has retryable defects: four capitalisation typos on
provenance values used to produce a terminal stop, because the enum check returned before the anchor was
counted. The guard is uniform over a pass rather than attached to each check, because the previous
version *was* attached to one check and missed the next case. Second, terminals are evaluated on the
Author's interpretation; a reviewer that anchors nothing produces
`E_REVIEWER_RECONSTRUCTION_UNUSABLE` and a fresh-reviewer retry, not a stop that blames the item.

That second policy needs a distinction to be correct rather than merely safe, and the first version of
it was wrong. Suppressing the reviewer's terminals wholesale discards the reviewer's `moves_surface: true`,
which is precisely the input the cross-side check consumes — the two fixes cancelled. The criterion that
makes both work is **assertion versus absence**, and it is decidable from the source rather than from a
judgment about what a code is "about":

| Trigger | Fires on | Portable between artifacts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assertion` | a value the Author wrote — `moves_surface: true`, `filled_from: unresolved`, two written values differing | yes; an assertion is attributable, so it means the same thing wherever it is found |
| `absence` | nothing written — no part declared `stated` or `stated_unverified` | no; "the item states nothing" and "this reading found nothing" are indistinguishable from one artifact |

An earlier version of this split keyed on "the reconstruction's own adequacy versus a property of the
item". That classified the same codes correctly and was undecidable from the source — and the tell was
that it called `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED` an adequacy code while the code's own name, its message, and the
failure-mode table all called it a property of the item. Three places said item, the list said adequacy.
That was a naming bug rather than a classification bug: the two readings are now two codes, and each
name is accurate.

Every terminal code declares its trigger, and the suite tests the declaration against behaviour with
five portability assertions — because an assertion in a comment is the same shape as the exemption that
hid a bug for two commits.

**This is not a separate stage.** It is what stage 2 was already doing, named, plus one comparison at
the review-and-freeze step. Reconstruction has a decent claim to its own persisted state, but the
promotion rule wants a diagnosed failure class across two pilot runs and there have been no pilot runs.

The honest counterweight belongs next to that, as the thing to watch: reconstruction now has its own
linter pass, its own actor pair, its own code prefix, its own escalation family, and its own stop state,
and it is the largest thing inside any stage. If a pilot diagnoses a reconstruction failure class twice,
the promotion evidence will already be sitting here.

### The reconstruction is the ceiling on everything after it

Every slice after this one verifies against the frozen bundle, so a faithful implementation of a wrong
reconstruction passes every gate and reports `ready_for_merge`. TICK gives that outcome its shape: a
response that fabricated its sources answered 9 of 10 generated checklist questions YES and scored 2/5
from a human annotator (`checklist--cook-2024:1961`), because the generated checklist inherited the
instruction's false premise (`:1878`).

The authors' conclusion has to be quoted whole, because an earlier version of this section cut it in a
direction that flattered the argument. It reads: generated-checklist answers "alone should not be used
to score responses **in human evaluation**, but also showing that **human evaluators are robust to
unhelpful or misleading checklists**" (`:1883`). Both restored clauses matter. The scope qualifier is
material — the finding is about human annotators working from a generated checklist, whereas this
pipeline's gates are mechanical checks and a model reviewer, so "this workflow does exactly that" was
too quick. And the second clause is evidence *for* one of the three mitigations rather than against it:
the annotator scored 2/5 correctly while answering 9 of 10 YES, which is the offline hand-graded sample
working. Independent reconstruction, declared support, and that sample are the mitigations; none is a
solution, and the sample is the one with a data point behind it.

## The `interpretation` block

It is carried inside the manifest rather than in a side file because it is normative. `claims[]`
descend from it, and freezing a bundle whose reconstruction was not frozen with it would leave the
run's definition of the goal mutable after the freeze. The manifest that carries it is defined in
[`the-boundary-bundle`](the-boundary-bundle.md); the block's own schema is defined here and is not
restated there.

| Field | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `goal.statement`, `problem.statement` | What the item is for; what is wrong or missing now |
| `provenance` on each | `stated` \| `stated_unverified` \| `inferred` \| `contradicted` |
| `support[]` on each | Typed pointers, below |
| `claim_provenance{}` | Keyed by claim id, valued by the same `provenance` plus `support[]` shape |
| `corrections[]` | One per place the item asserts something the repository contradicts |
| `gaps[]` | One per element the item did not supply |

`claim_provenance` is a map rather than a field on each claim for a reason that is not cosmetic: the
same block is written by two actors. The Author writes one into the manifest, and the
Boundary-reviewer writes a **standalone** one at the review step with no entries and no claims list. One
shape means one set of rules and one linter for both, and it means the reviewer's artifact is not a
partial boundary.

The provenance values:

| Value | Means | Requires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stated` | the item says it and resolution corroborated it | at least one `item_locator` |
| `stated_unverified` | the item says it and resolution could neither corroborate nor contradict it | at least one `item_locator`, and no external support — the absence is the point |
| `inferred` | the repository, logs, or history supply it | at least one pointer that is **not** an `item_locator` |
| `contradicted` | the item asserts it and the repository shows otherwise | as `inferred`, plus a matching `corrections[]` entry |

Support pointers are typed, because an untyped citation is unverifiable: `item_locator`, `repo_path`,
`log_query`, `commit`, `registry_entry`. The two rules that follow are the ones that do the work — a
`stated` claim must carry an `item_locator`, and an inference whose only support is the item it was not
in cites nothing.

**A locator is checked for presence, never for resolution, and that is the weakest point in the whole
provenance system.** The Linter does not read the item — it cannot, since the item lives behind a
tracker adapter — so `description#4` on a two-paragraph item lints exactly as clean as a true citation.
Every rule here establishes that a citation was *written*, not that it points at anything. The domain
that would make resolution checkable is supplied by the tracker adapter and is specified in
[`tracker-and-forge-ports`](tracker-and-forge-ports.md).

The consequence is worse than "cheap to fake by accident", which is how an earlier version of this
paragraph put it. The check did not merely fail to detect divergence — it **affirmatively reported
concurrence**. An author reading of "exports are too slow for large accounts" and a reviewer reading of
"the retry button double-submits and corrupts the manifest", both citing `description#1`, recorded a
`pass`, and the stage reads that as *the two readings are anchored together*. The
manufactured-agreement failure, reproduced inside the check built to detect it.

Two fixes, and neither needs the adapter. **This check now refutes or abstains and never passes** — a
`pass` was the only affirmatively misleading outcome available to it. And the existing exemption is
widened rather than joined by a new rule: it already abstains when either side cites nothing, on the
grounds that the comparison has no domain, and one identical locator on each side is the same
condition — a set with no discriminating power, where identical and opposite readings are
indistinguishable.

Resolving locators against a real part list, once the adapter supplies one, does **not** rescue the
degenerate overlap case. Two reconstructions both citing a *valid* `description#1` are still
indistinguishable from each other, which is why `abstain` exists and why there is still no diversity
metric.

Two residuals, stated rather than checked. A side resting on one locator while the other cites three
still reports overlap; drawing that line needs a diversity metric, and the semantic differential is the
real check rather than something worth propping up. And a whole interpretation — goal, problem, and
every claim — can rest on one default locator with nothing flagging it.

`corrections[]` carries `about` (a claim id or the literal `goal` or `problem`), `item_assertion`,
`repo_finding`, `support[]`, `resolution` (`item_wrong` | `repo_changed_since` | `ambiguous`), and
`moves_surface`. `gaps[]` carries `element` and `filled_from`, which is either a support pointer or the
literal `unresolved`.

**`stated_unverified` constrains the obligation graph.** A `must` that traces a `stated_unverified`
claim **at all** is rejected: it gates partly on an item assertion nothing corroborates. Verify the
claim, drop the trace if a coupling edge is the real anchor, or author the obligation as `watch`.

The predicate is "cites an uncorroborated claim" and not "has no corroborated anchor", because the
weaker form was defeated by adding a single coupling-edge trace — and since `entails` requires every
coupling edge to be covered, coupling traces are the normal case rather than an exotic one. The prose
said the rule caught a must that gates on an uncorroborated assertion; the code asked whether the entry
had any corroborated anchor at all. Those differ exactly when an entry has both, and a coupling edge is
a different anchor rather than corroboration of the claim.

That member and that rule came out of transcribing the pre-schema worked example, which carried
`regression since ~July — unverified secondhand`. A three-member enum could record the first half of
that sentence and not the second, so an assertion resolution could not confirm looked identical to one
it did. The source had already solved the consequence without naming the cause: its `C2` grounds a
`watch` entry and gates nothing.

`filled_from: unresolved` means **established** unsettleable and never "not filled in yet", so it
requires a non-empty `sought[]` of typed pointers that were checked and did not settle it. Without that
the literal did double duty and an honest first-draft placeholder ended the run with no round available
to replace it — while a *wrong* pointer continued it. A missing `sought[]` is retryable, which the
suppression policy then keeps from terminating.

`W_ANCHOR_DISJOINT` is the one warning. Two reconstructions citing no item locator in common may be
reading different requirements, but locator overlap is not reading agreement in either direction, and no
authoring round can fix a disjoint reading. So it is recorded and requires the semantic divergence test
rather than standing in for it.

## In the run

The Author's pass, before any mechanism work is paid for:

- Author: reads the item alone and records what it says — goal, problem, numbered claims — each with an `item_locator` pointing at the part of the item that says it
- Author: does this pass first and separately because provenance is otherwise unrecoverable — read the item and the repository together and nothing afterwards can say which of them told you
- Author: resolves each claim against read-only repo, logs, and deploy history; quantifies vague terms from data
- Author: sets provenance from that resolution — `stated` where corroborated, `stated_unverified` where neither corroborated nor contradicted, `contradicted` where the repository shows otherwise — and adds `inferred` entries for anything the item never mentioned
- Author: writes one `corrections[]` entry per contradicted part, naming the item's assertion, the repository's finding, its support, a resolution, and whether the correction **moves the change surface**
- Author: writes one `gaps[]` entry per element the item did not supply, naming what it was filled from, or the literal `unresolved` where nothing can settle it
- Linter (no model): lints the interpretation on its own, before any mechanism work is paid for, and reports terminal findings separately from fixable ones
- Orchestrator (no model): on an **assertion**-triggered terminal finding — appends the reason code, calls `attach_reference` so the drafted interpretation reaches the item as the run's product, finalizes the lease, stops; it consumes no lint round, because no further authoring round can change it
- Orchestrator (no model): on the **provisional** finding that nothing in the reconstruction is anchored — skips the mechanism sketch, the coupling analysis, and the registry pass, and goes straight to the independent reading with the interpretation alone; the spend stops here and the run does not

The independent reading, which is the counterweight the whole slice rests on:

- Orchestrator (no model): starts Boundary-reviewer in a fresh session, cross-family from the Author
- Orchestrator (no model): gives it the item text and read-only repo access and **withholds the boundary**, so its reading of the item is not anchored on the Author's
- Boundary-reviewer: writes its own standalone `interpretation` — goal, problem, claims, provenance, typed support — under the same rules and the same linter
- Linter (no model): lints the reviewer's side under the same rules; where the Author anchored and the reviewer did not, that is `E_REVIEWER_RECONSTRUCTION_UNUSABLE` and a fresh-reviewer retry, because an absence on the reviewer's side is a statement about the reviewer
- Linter (no model): resolves the Author's provisional absence against the reviewer's — **both unanchored** is `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED`, corroborated by two blind cross-family readings and now genuinely a property of the item; **Author unanchored, reviewer anchored** is `E_AUTHOR_RECONSTRUCTION_INADEQUATE`, and the Author re-authors against the reviewer's locators
- Linter (no model): does not call the reviewer's absence a reviewer defect when the Author is also unanchored, because there it is the corroboration rather than an indictment — treating it as a defect made it a retryable finding, which then suppressed the very conclusion it corroborates
- Linter (no model): compares the two — warns `W_ANCHOR_DISJOINT` when their `stated` and `stated_unverified` parts cite no item locator in common, and reports `X_MOVES_SURFACE_DISPUTED` when the two sides disagree about whether correcting the same thing moves the change surface
- Boundary-reviewer: then receives the Author's interpretation and describes one change that satisfies its own reading of the goal while failing the Author's, or returns `readings_agree`
- Orchestrator (no model): on a described divergence — escalates `intent_ambiguous` and attaches both interpretations; two defensible readings mean the choice between them has an owner

> **The divergence test is weak, the calibration is a guess, and the guess was anchored to the wrong
> condition.** Song reports two numbers. Where evaluators generate rubrics independently *including
> their structure*, "agreement collapses to near-random levels (r̄ ≈ 0.24)"
> (`judge-ceiling--song-2026-tencent--evaluation-illusion:87`); standardising the instrument alone
> raises it to r̄ ≈ 0.62 (`:894`, `:1041`). An earlier version of this note reasoned from 0.24 — expect
> near-random divergence, so any similarity threshold escalates everything, so make both halves weak.
> But this design **mandates a shared instrument**: both sides use the same `interpretation` shape, the
> same provenance enum, the same support kinds, the same linter. That is the 0.62 condition, not the
> 0.24 one.
>
> Two consequences, both from the same citation. Expected divergence is materially lower than assumed,
> so the test could afford to be stronger than it is — the escalate-everything fear was calibrated to a
> condition this design does not create. And `readings_agree` is **weaker** evidence than a first reading
> suggests: Song's point is that 62% of agreement is attributable to the shared instrument rather than
> shared judgment, so agreement between two sides using an identical schema is substantially
> manufactured by the schema. Which is the sharper form of the warning, and an argument for keeping the
> two halves weak on a different ground than the one originally given — not because divergence is
> expected to be everywhere, but because agreement proves less than it looks like it does.
>
> What escalation rate this produces is unknown, and it remains the most likely reason this slice needs
> retuning.

## Codes this slice owns

Terminal, reaching `interpretation_blocked`: `X_GAP_UNRESOLVABLE`, `X_QUANTITY_ASSUMED`,
`X_CORRECTION_CHANGES_SCOPE`, `X_RECONSTRUCTION_UNANCHORED`, `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED`,
`X_MOVES_SURFACE_DISPUTED`.

Two limits on `X_ITEM_UNANCHORED` specifically, both real: it detects the total absence of item
anchoring rather than weak anchoring, and it is deliberately not reached from a badly-cited or
badly-typed `stated` claim, because letting a retryable failure decide a terminal one is how a run stops
for the wrong reason.

Retryable: `E_REVIEWER_RECONSTRUCTION_UNUSABLE` and `E_AUTHOR_RECONSTRUCTION_INADEQUATE`. Both are
retries under `MAX_BOUNDARY_ROUNDS` rather than stops, and they exist so that a failure by either
reconstructor is never reported as a property of the item.

Warning: `W_ANCHOR_DISJOINT`.

The prefix contract, the outcome set including `provisional`, and the stop states are defined in
[`autonomous-workitem-workflow`](autonomous-workitem-workflow.md).

4	/**
5	 * Reference linter for the boundary bundle. The specification was one document and is

875	          add('E_QUANTITY_NO_PROVENANCE', at,
876	            'a quantitative entry must declare quantity.filled_from as a typed support pointer or the literal '
877	            + `unresolved; without it ${JSON.stringify(q.value)} cites nothing at the point it is used`);
878	        } else {
879	          ok('E_QUANTITY_NO_PROVENANCE', at);
880	          ok('X_QUANTITY_ASSUMED', at);
881	        }
882	      }
883	    } else if (e.quantitative !== false) {
884	      add('E_QUANTITATIVE_NOT_BOOLEAN', at, 'quantitative must be true or false');
885	    }
886	
887	    if (isGating(e)) {
888	      if (TEST_ROLE.includes(e.test_role)) ok('E_TESTROLE_REQUIRED', at);
889	      else add('E_TESTROLE_REQUIRED', at, `mechanical + pre_merge + must requires test_role of ${TEST_ROLE.join(' | ')}`);
890	      if (BASELINE.includes(e.baseline)) ok('E_BASELINE_REQUIRED', at);
891	      else add('E_BASELINE_REQUIRED', at, `mechanical + pre_merge + must requires baseline of ${BASELINE.join(' | ')}`);
892	      if (BASELINE.includes(e.baseline) && TEST_ROLE.includes(e.test_role)
893	          && BASELINE_ROLE[e.baseline] !== e.test_role) {
894	        add('E_BASELINE_ROLE_MISMATCH', at,
895	          `baseline ${e.baseline} is only legal with test_role ${BASELINE_ROLE[e.baseline]}`);
896	      }
897	      if (e.baseline === 'expected_error' && (!e.error_code || !e.error_pattern)) {
898	        add('E_EXPECTED_ERROR_UNTYPED', at, 'baseline expected_error requires error_code and error_pattern');
899	      }
900	    } else if (e.test_role !== undefined || e.baseline !== undefined) {
901	      add('E_TESTROLE_FORBIDDEN', at,
902	        'test_role and baseline are only meaningful on mechanical + pre_merge + must');
903	    }
904	    if (e.evidence !== undefined) {
905	      add('E_EVIDENCE_IN_MANIFEST', at,
906	        'evidence edges are a stage-4 artifact and cannot be fields of a manifest frozen at stage 3');
907	    }
908	
909	    const m = Array.isArray(e.mandate) ? e.mandate : [];
910	    if (m.length === 0) add('E_ORPHAN_ENTRY', at, 'entry maps to no mandate');
911	    m.forEach((name) => {
912	      mandatesUsed.add(name);
913	      if (!mandates.includes(name)) add('E_UNKNOWN_MANDATE', at, `mandate ${name} is not declared in /mandates`);
914	      else ok('E_UNKNOWN_MANDATE', at);
915	    });
916	
917	    // traces anchor an obligation to a requirement stated outside the boundary
918	    const tr = Array.isArray(e.traces) ? e.traces : [];
919	    if (tr.length === 0) add('E_NO_TRACE', at, 'entry has no traces'); else ok('E_NO_TRACE', at);
920	    let upstream = 0;
921	    const uncorroborated = [];
922	    tr.forEach((t) => {
923	      const self = t === e.id;
924	      const isSelection = selected.has(t);
925	      if (!claimIds.has(t) && !couplingIds.has(t) && !entryIds.has(t)) {
926	        add('E_TRACE_UNRESOLVED', at, `trace ${t} resolves to no claim, coupling edge, or entry`);
927	        return;
928	      }
929	      if (self && !isSelection) {
930	        add('E_SELF_TRACE', at,
931	          `trace ${t} is the entry's own id and the entry is not declared registry-selected, so it anchors nothing`);
932	        return;
933	      }
934	      if (self && isSelection) {
935	        // Visible on purpose. When this exemption was silent it read exactly like
936	        // approval, which is how a per-issue entry wearing a registry-shaped id
937	        // passed two rules unnoticed.
938	        R.exempt('E_SELF_TRACE', at,
939	          `self-trace exempted because ${t} is declared in registry_selections`);
940	      } else {
941	        ok('E_SELF_TRACE', at);
942	      }
943	      if (claimIds.has(t) || couplingIds.has(t) || (self && isSelection)) upstream += 1;
944	      // A claim the resolution pass could neither corroborate nor contradict is
945	      // still an anchor; it is just not one a gating obligation can rest on.
946	      if (claimIds.has(t) && unverifiedClaims.has(t)) uncorroborated.push(t);
947	    });
948	    if (tr.length > 0 && upstream === 0) {
949	      add('E_NO_UPSTREAM_TRACE', at,
950	        'at least one trace must reach a claim, a coupling edge, or this entry as a declared registry '
951	        + 'selection; tracing only other obligations records a relationship and does not anchor');
952	    }
953	    // Provenance constrains the obligation graph. The predicate is "cites an
954	    // uncorroborated claim at all", not "has no corroborated anchor": the weaker
955	    // form was defeated by adding one coupling-edge trace, and coupling traces are
956	    // the normal case rather than an exotic one. A coupling edge is a different
957	    // anchor, not corroboration of the claim.
958	    if (e.obligation === 'must') {
959	      if (uncorroborated.length === 0) ok('E_UNVERIFIED_GROUNDS_MUST', at);
960	      else {
961	        add('E_UNVERIFIED_GROUNDS_MUST', at,
962	          `this must traces ${uncorroborated.join(', ')}, declared stated_unverified, so it gates partly on an `
963	          + 'item assertion nothing corroborates; verify the claim, drop the trace if a coupling edge is the '
964	          + 'real anchor, or author the obligation as watch');
965	      }
966	    }
967	  });
968	
969	  mandates.forEach((name) => {
970	    if (!mandatesUsed.has(name)) add('E_UNANCHORED_MANDATE', '/mandates', `mandate ${name} has no entry`);
971	  });
972	
973	  // entails: every coupling edge covered, and no key outside the coupling space
974	  coupling.forEach((c, i) => {
975	    if (!c || !c.id) return;
976	    const at = `/coupling/${i} (${c.id})`;
977	    if (!(c.id in entails)) {
978	      add('E_ENTAILS_UNDECLARED', at, `coupling edge ${c.id} is neither mapped in /entails nor marked uncovered`);
979	      return;
980	    }
981	    const target = entails[c.id];
982	    if (target !== 'uncovered' && !entryIds.has(target)) {
983	      add('E_ENTAILS_UNRESOLVED', at, `/entails/${c.id} points at ${target}, which is not an entry id`);
984	    } else ok('E_ENTAILS_UNRESOLVED', at);
985	  });
986	  Object.keys(entails).forEach((k) => {
987	    if (!couplingIds.has(k)) {
988	      add('E_ENTAILS_ALIEN_KEY', `/entails/${k === '' ? '""' : k}`,
989	        `${k === '' ? 'empty key' : k} is not a coupling edge id; a typo here would otherwise read as coverage`);
990	    }
991	  });
992	
993	  return suppressTerminals(f);
994	}
995	
996	/** Stage 5. Runs once tests exist, against the frozen boundary. */
997	function lintEvidence(boundary, ev, opts = {}) {
998	  const R = recorder();
999	  const f = R.all;
1000	  const add = R.add;
1001	  const ok = R.ok;
1002	  if (!ev || typeof ev !== 'object') {
1003	    add('E_NOT_A_MAPPING', '/', 'evidence did not parse to a mapping');
1004	    return f;
1005	  }
1006	  const entries = Array.isArray(boundary.entries) ? boundary.entries : [];
1007	  const byId = new Map(entries.filter((e) => e && e.id).map((e) => [e.id, e]));
1008	  const gating = entries.filter((e) => e && isGating(e));
1009	  const edges = Array.isArray(ev.edges) ? ev.edges : [];
1010	  if (opts.collectedCases !== null && opts.collectedCases !== undefined
1011	      && !Array.isArray(opts.collectedCases)) {
1012	    throw new TypeError(
1013	      'collectedCases must be an array of collected test case ids or omitted; omitting it declares '
1014	      + 'no-domain, and passing the wrong shape would silently do the same.',
1015	    );
1016	  }
1017	  const collected = Array.isArray(opts.collectedCases) ? new Set(opts.collectedCases.map(String)) : null;
1018	
1019	  if (!ev.boundary_digest) {
1020	    add('E_NO_BOUNDARY_DIGEST', '/boundary_digest',
1021	      'evidence must name the frozen bundle digest it was written against');
1022	  } else ok('E_NO_BOUNDARY_DIGEST', '/boundary_digest');
1023	
1024	  const covered = new Set();
1025	  const caseBaselines = new Map();
1026	  edges.forEach((edge, i) => {
1027	    const at = `/edges/${i}`;
1028	    if (!edge || !edge.entry) { add('E_EDGE_NO_ENTRY', at, 'edge names no entry'); return; }
1029	    if (!byId.has(edge.entry)) {
1030	      add('E_EDGE_UNKNOWN_ENTRY', at, `edge names ${edge.entry}, which is not an entry in the boundary`);
1031	      return;
1032	    }
1033	    const e = byId.get(edge.entry);
1034	    if (!isGating(e)) {
1035	      add('E_EDGE_ON_NONGATING', at,
1036	        `${edge.entry} is not mechanical + pre_merge + must, so it takes no test evidence`);
1037	      return;
1038	    }
1039	    if (!edge.case_id) {
1040	      add('E_EDGE_NO_CASE_ID', at, 'edge must name a collected test case id, not a file');
1041	      return;
1042	    }
1043	    ok('E_EDGE_NO_CASE_ID', at);
1044	    // Collectability. The list of ids the runner actually collected is supplied by
1045	    // the caller — a fixture here, the runner in production — so the membership
1046	    // check exists and is tested before the runner does.
1047	    if (collected === null) {
1048	      R.exempt('E_EDGE_CASE_NOT_COLLECTED', at,
1049	        'no collected-case list was supplied, so an edge can be checked for naming a case id but not for '
1050	        + "naming one that exists; this is the runner's input and its absence is declared rather than assumed");
1051	    } else if (collected.has(String(edge.case_id))) {
1052	      ok('E_EDGE_CASE_NOT_COLLECTED', at);
1053	    } else {
1054	      add('E_EDGE_CASE_NOT_COLLECTED', at,
1055	        `${edge.case_id} is not a case the runner collected, so this entry's evidence is a phantom: the `
1056	        + 'gate would report a pass for a test that never ran');
1057	    }
1058	    covered.add(edge.entry);
1059	    if (!caseBaselines.has(edge.case_id)) caseBaselines.set(edge.case_id, []);
1060	    caseBaselines.get(edge.case_id).push({ at, baseline: e.baseline });
1061	
1062	    if (e.test_role === 'preservation'
1063	        && (!edge.probe || !PROBE_KIND.includes(edge.probe.kind) || !edge.probe.ref)) {
1064	      add('E_NO_SENSITIVITY_PROBE', at,
1065	        `${edge.entry} is preservation, so the edge requires probe.kind of ${PROBE_KIND.join(' | ')} with a ref, `
1066	        + 'or the entry must be reclassified as independent_review');
1067	    } else if (e.test_role === 'preservation') {
1068	      ok('E_NO_SENSITIVITY_PROBE', at);
1069	    }
1070	  });
1071	
1072	  gating.forEach((e) => {
1073	    if (!covered.has(e.id)) {
1074	      add('E_NO_EVIDENCE_EDGE', `/edges (${e.id})`, `gating entry ${e.id} has no evidence edge`);
1075	    }
1076	  });
1077	
1078	  for (const [caseId, list] of caseBaselines) {
1079	    const distinct = [...new Set(list.map((x) => x.baseline))];
1080	    if (distinct.length > 1) {
1081	      add('E_EDGE_BASELINE_CONFLICT', list.map((x) => x.at).join(', '),
1082	        `test case ${caseId} carries conflicting baselines: ${distinct.join(', ')}`);
1083	    }
1084	  }
1085	  return f;
1086	}
1087	
1088	function main(argv) {
1089	  const args = argv.slice(2);
1090	  const evIdx = args.indexOf('--evidence');
1091	  const evFile = evIdx >= 0 ? args[evIdx + 1] : null;
1092	  const files = evIdx >= 0 ? args.slice(0, evIdx) : args;
1093	  if (files.length === 0) {
1094	    process.stderr.write('usage: lint-boundary.js <boundary.yaml> [...] [--evidence <evidence.yaml>]\n');
1095	    return 2;
1096	  }
1097	  let bad = 0;
1098	  for (const file of files) {
1099	    let findings;
1100	    let warned = [];
1101	    let doc = null;
1102	    try {
1103	      doc = load(file);
1104	      const records = lintBoundary(doc);
1105	      findings = failures(records);
1106	      warned = warnings(records);
1107	      if (evFile && files.length === 1) findings = findings.concat(failures(lintEvidence(doc, load(evFile))));
1108	    } catch (err) {
1109	      findings = [{ code: 'E_PARSE', at: '/', message: err.message }];
1110	    }
1111	    const name = path.basename(file);
1112	    for (const w of warned) process.stdout.write(`warn  ${name}  ${w.code}  ${w.at}\n        ${w.message}\n`);
1113	    if (findings.length === 0) process.stdout.write(`ok    ${name}\n`);
1114	    else {
1115	      bad += 1;
1116	      const term = findings.filter((x) => isTerminal(x.code)).length;
1117	      process.stdout.write(`FAIL  ${name}  (${findings.length}${term ? `, ${term} terminal` : ''})\n`);
1118	      for (const x of findings) {
1119	        // Terminal findings are marked because the caller's response differs: a
1120	        // fixable finding earns another lint round, a terminal one ends the run.
1121	        process.stdout.write(`        ${isTerminal(x.code) ? 'TERMINAL ' : ''}${x.code}  ${x.at}\n`);
1122	        process.stdout.write(`          ${x.message}\n`);
1123	      }
1124	    }
1125	  }
1126	  return bad === 0 ? 0 : 1;
1127	}
1128	
1129	module.exports = {
1130	  lintBoundary, lintInterpretationPair, lintEvidence, load, isGating, failures,
1131	  warnings, provisionals, abstentions, fired, isTerminal, isWarning, suppressTerminals,
1132	  CODES, TERMINAL, WARNING, TERMINAL_TRIGGER, ABSENCE_TRIGGERED,
1133	};
1134	
1135	if (require.main === module) process.exit(main(process.argv));
1136

content.content:
# The item's addressable parts, as the tracker adapter's `read(ref)` would return
# them. Supplied to the linter so an `item_locator` can be checked for RESOLUTION
# and not merely for presence.
#
# Fixture-declared here, adapter-supplied in production. The check is written and
# tested now; the infrastructure later feeds an already-tested check instead of
# arriving alongside an untested one. Circular while the author writes both, and
# non-circular for free once the adapter produces it — with no rewrite.
item: WI-1234
parts:
  - description#1
  - description#2
  - comment#1
  - comment#2
=========== valid.yaml ===========
schema_version: 1
tracker: jira
item: WI-1234
registry_revision: "9f2c1ab"
registry_selections: [INV-2]
mandates: [data-integrity, correctness, resource]
non_goals:
  - "retry button behaviour — tracked as JIRA-1250"
interpretation:
  # A deliberately unrefined item: it states a symptom, no goal, no numbers, and
  # one thing that is not true. Every one of those is recorded rather than
  # smoothed over, which is the whole point of the block.
  goal:
    statement: "a large-account export either completes or leaves the destination unchanged"
    provenance: inferred
    support:
      - kind: repo_path
        ref: "services/export/writer.py"
      - kind: log_query
        ref: "export.status=FAILED AND rows_written>0, last 30d"
  problem:
    statement: "large-account exports time out at the gateway and leave a partial file behind"
    provenance: stated
    support:
      - kind: item_locator
        ref: "description#1"
      - kind: log_query
        ref: "export.duration_ms p99 by account_size, last 30d"
  claim_provenance:
    C1:
      provenance: stated
      support:
        - kind: item_locator
          ref: "description#1"
    C3:
      # The item says the leftover file is empty. It is not — it holds the rows
      # written before the timeout. The obligation reads the same either way,
      # which is what moves_surface: false records below.
      provenance: contradicted
      support:
        - kind: log_query
          ref: "export.rows_written WHERE status=FAILED, last 30d"
        - kind: repo_path
          ref: "services/export/writer.py"
  corrections:
    - about: C3
      item_assertion: "an empty file is left behind on hang"
      repo_finding: "the file left behind holds the rows written before the timeout, not zero rows"
      resolution: item_wrong
      moves_surface: false
      support:
        - kind: log_query
          ref: "export.rows_written WHERE status=FAILED, last 30d"
  gaps:
    # AC-1 asserts 240 seconds and the item supplies no number at all. The
    # enforcement is quantity.filled_from on AC-1 itself; this entry is the
    # summary. Emptying gaps[] used to leave the threshold standing and clean,
    # which made this list decorative.
    - element: "the completion budget for a large export"
      filled_from:
        kind: repo_path
        ref: "infra/gateway/timeouts.yaml"
    - element: "what counts as a large account"
      filled_from:
        kind: log_query
        ref: "row_count percentiles by account, last 90d"
claims:
  - id: C1
    text: "exports fail for large accounts"
  - id: C3
    text: "empty file left behind on hang"
coupling:
  - id: CPL-1
    kind: consumer
    target: "jobs/reconcile.py"
  - id: CPL-2
    kind: metric
    target: "dashboards/export.json"
entails:
  CPL-1: PRES-1
  CPL-2: PRES-2
entries:
  - id: INV-2
    statement: "destination holds a file only if its row count equals the manifest"
    verifier: mechanical
    verification_stage: pre_merge
    obligation: must
    mandate: [data-integrity]
    traces: [C3, INV-2]
    observation: "force a timeout mid-export, list the destination"
    decision: "no file present, or row count equals manifest"
    quantitative: false
    test_role: change
    baseline: assertion_fail
  - id: PRES-1
    statement: "the reconcile job completes against every terminal export state"
    verifier: mechanical
    verification_stage: pre_merge
    obligation: must
    mandate: [correctness]
    traces: [CPL-1]
    observation: "run reconcile against a destination with no file"
    decision: "exit code 0"
    quantitative: false
    test_role: preservation
    baseline: pass
  - id: AC-1
    statement: "export of 500k rows completes inside the gateway budget"
    verifier: mechanical
    verification_stage: pre_merge
    obligation: must
    mandate: [correctness]
    traces: [C1]
    observation: "run a 500k export against staging, warm cache"
    decision: "terminal status SUCCEEDED within the stated budget"
    quantitative: true
    quantity:
      value: "240"
      unit: "seconds"
      conditions: "staging, warm cache, single concurrent export, 500k rows"
      filled_from:
        kind: repo_path
        ref: "infra/gateway/timeouts.yaml"
    test_role: change
    baseline: assertion_fail
  - id: AC-4
    statement: "peak RSS stays within the stated ratio of the 50k baseline in production"
    verifier: mechanical
    verification_stage: production
    obligation: must
    mandate: [resource]
    traces: [C1]
    observation: "production RSS metric over 24h"
    decision: "ratio within the stated bound"
    quantitative: true
    quantity:
      value: "1.50"
      unit: "ratio to the 50k peak"
      conditions: "production, 24h window, p99"
      filled_from:
        kind: log_query
        ref: "export.rss.p99 at 50k rows, last 90d"
    handoff:
      owner: "platform-oncall"
      trigger: "24h after deploy"
      verification_method: "grafana panel export.rss.p99"
      evidence_destination: "runs/WI-1234/handoff/"
      failure_transition: "reopen WI-1234"
  - id: PRES-2
    statement: "alert EXP-1 fires on the same conditions after the status change"
    verifier: mechanical
    verification_stage: pre_merge
    obligation: must
    mandate: [correctness]
    traces: [CPL-2]
    observation: "replay the alert expression against both status vocabularies"
    decision: "same firing set"
    quantitative: false
    test_role: preservation
    baseline: pass
  - id: AC-7
    statement: "the reconcile job's first post-merge run consumes every terminal state"
    verifier: independent_review
    verification_stage: post_merge
    obligation: must
    mandate: [correctness]
    traces: [CPL-1]
    observation: "read the first nightly reconcile log after merge"
    decision: "no unhandled terminal state"
    quantitative: false
    handoff:
      owner: "data-platform"
      trigger: "first nightly reconcile after merge"
      verification_method: "reconcile job exit status and unhandled-state counter"
      evidence_destination: "runs/WI-1234/handoff/"
      failure_transition: "reopen WI-1234 and revert the status enum"
  - id: W-1
    statement: "export duration trend does not regress"
    verifier: observation
    verification_stage: production
    obligation: watch
    mandate: [resource]
    traces: [C1]
    observation: "export.duration_ms p99 weekly"
    decision: "recorded, not gated"
    quantitative: false

# Implementation notes — gh-158

NOT NORMATIVE. Not referenced by the boundary and not part of it.

Refinement states what must be true. How to build it is the next phase, and these
are notes for that phase. Nothing here gates anything.

## Change surface

```
modus/prompts/author-boundary.md               the Author's drafting prompt
modus/scripts/draft-boundary.js                renders it, validates the result
modus/scripts/__tests__/draft-boundary.test.js
boundary/gh-158.yaml, boundary/gh-158.sketch.md   this boundary itself
```

Anything else is out of scope.

## Input

The script does **not** fetch from any tracker. Fetching is adapter work and belongs
to gh-156. Input arrives as a JSON document on a path or on stdin:

```json
{
  "item_ref": "gh-158",
  "tracker": "github-issues",
  "parts": [
    { "id": "description#1", "text": "..." },
    { "id": "description#2", "text": "..." }
  ]
}
```

`parts[].id` is `<field>#<n>`, one-based, paragraph-level within a field. Paragraph
granularity is the working answer and it is known to be inadequate for short items —
see `domestique-3lf`. The script does not invent parts, split sentences, or reorder
them; it addresses what it is given.

## Output

Writes `boundary/<item_ref>.yaml`. Refuses to overwrite an existing file unless
`--force` is passed. A silent overwrite of a frozen boundary would remove the
freeze without recording that it happened.

Drafts a **candidate only**. It never approves, never freezes, never commits, and
never marks a boundary frozen. A human does that, per gh-158's own goal.

## Validation

Requires `modus/scripts/lint-boundary.js` and calls `lintBoundary(doc, { itemParts })`
with `itemParts` taken from the input's `parts[].id`. Passing the part list is
required, not optional: without it every `item_locator` check exempts itself and the
draft is unvalidated where it matters most.

Exit codes follow the three-outcome rule in the modus README:

| Exit | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | draft written, lints with no failures |
| `1` | draft written, lints with failures — they are printed and the file is kept for editing |
| `2` | could not run: input unreadable, malformed, or no parts supplied. Names the cause. Writes nothing |

Exit `2` writes nothing. A partial file at the boundary path would be read by the
next step as a boundary.

## Semantic correspondence

The anti-boilerplate requirement, and the reason AC-1 and AC-2 in the manifest are
not sufficient on their own.

- Every `claims[].id` referenced in `interpretation.claim_provenance` carries at least
  one `item_locator` support whose `ref` resolves to a supplied part.
- Changing the text of an input part changes the drafted `goal`, `problem`, or at least
  one claim. A draft that is invariant under its input is boilerplate wearing a schema.
- Copying input text into a comment or an unread field does not satisfy either rule.

The tests for this are mutation tests: perturb one input part, assert the named output
fields differ. An adversarial fixture — a static, well-formed, gh-158-shaped manifest
that ignores its input entirely — must fail them.
